props.title: Confessions
lines: Housel publishes his own household rules so the book is not a lecture from nowhere.
Independence is the goal. The strategy is whatever you will actually stick with.

props.title: Not a universal prescription

rows.v: Independence. Every saving and investing decision is pointed at not being a forced actor.
They keep a paid-for house as a large, conservative chunk — a reasonable, not maximally rational, choice.
Around 20% of assets outside the house in a mix they can hold. No leverage.
He prefers low-cost index funds and notes about 85% of large active funds fail to beat their index over long spans.
The plan is what his family will stick with — not what a spreadsheet says is optimal this year.

props.note: Confessions chapter. His plan is not your plan.

props.title: A confession is not a command

rows.v: These are Housel's household rules. They are evidence of 'reasonable,' not a model portfolio.
Every dollar is aimed at not being forced — not at winning a neighbor's comparison.
A paid house plus about 20% of other assets, no leverage, index-heavy — chosen for stickiness.
He cites about 85% of large active funds missing the index over long spans as a reason for simplicity.

props.kicker: RECAP — THE BOOK ON ONE CARD
props.title: What to remember
items: Behaviour beats formulas; luck and risk are a pair.
Name enough. Compounding needs time and survival.
Tails drive returns; savings and unseen wealth are the real pile.
Be reasonable. Leave room for error. You will change.
Volatility is a fee. Do not copy another player's game.
Pessimism seduces. Stories fake control. Independence is the point.
props.closer: Education, not advice. Consult a SEBI-registered adviser. Thanks for watching.
